item.title: Project Zero's 30-day disclosure clock; Fed says 87% now rank AI the top risk
item.description: Google's Project Zero has replaced its 90-plus-30 disclosure policy with a fixed clock that reaches 30 days in January 2028, fix or no fix, because it says language models have collapsed the time between patch and exploit. The Federal Reserve's stability report puts AI at the top of its risk survey for the first time, with $680 billion of computing debt now a third of investment-grade issuance. The Wall Street Journal reports Washington will name more than two dozen AI 'national champions' for export, days before Trump meets Xi in Shenzhen on Thursday with chip curbs on the table and a US–China AI incident hotline still not operational. The FAA now blames a router feature and its contractor for Friday's ground stop, with zero evidence of an AI link; GXO signed for up to 1,000 Apptronik humanoids; Fractile raised $720 million at $7 billion before shipping a chip; and Datadog, Check Point and Corelight published the operational detail behind two agent-era threats.
item.content:encoded:
The one thing to know: Put a date field on your vulnerability tracker. From February 2 a Project Zero report becomes public 60 days after the vendor hears about it, and from January 2028 it is 30, whether or not a patch exists. If your SLA for operating systems, browsers and hypervisors is longer than that, the gap is now on a public schedule.

Project Zero scraps the 30-day soak period: bugs go public 90 days after reporting now, 60 from February 2, 30 from January 2028, fixed or not

Google's Project Zero published its 2026 disclosure policy on November 13, replacing the '90 + 30' rules in place since 2021 with 'Full X': details are released X days after the vendor is told, regardless of fix status, severity or variants. The team's stated reason is that LLM tooling lets attackers find bugs and turn patches into exploits almost immediately, so patch soak time is 'no longer meaningful', and that it now finds several vulnerabilities a week where it once found a few a year. Vendors objected that a hard clock would expose unfixed bugs and push them to fix Project Zero's reports ahead of worse ones; the phased schedule is the compromise. In-the-wild bugs stay on Google's seven-day policy.

  • Security: Measure your patch SLA for browsers, operating systems, hypervisors and common libraries against a 30-day total from vendor notification. Subscribe to Project Zero's Reporting Transparency list, which names the product within a week of the report, and map each entry against your inventory with its expected publication date.
  • Executives: Project Zero's policies became the industry norm in 2015 and 2021. Expect other researchers, AI bug-finding platforms and regulators to adopt the same clock, and ask vendors in the next review how fast they can ship a fix or a mitigation.
  • Developers: The mechanisms Project Zero says it expects vendors to build are feature flags, input filtering, authenticated alternate update channels and hotpatching. If you cannot turn a code path off in production without a release, start there.
  • ML engineers: The policy is a direct consequence of model-assisted vulnerability discovery scaling faster than fixing: the CSA notes only 97 of 1,596 AI-found open-source bugs reported under Project Glasswing had confirmed patches by May.
  • Beginners: Google's elite bug-hunting team will now publish details of a software flaw on a fixed timetable even if the maker has not fixed it, because AI has made attackers fast enough that waiting no longer protects anyone. The timetable shrinks to 30 days by 2028.

Source: Help Net Security · Cloud Security Alliance research note · Project Zero policy post

Fed Financial Stability Report: 87% of market contacts name AI the top risk, up from 50% in May; $680 billion of computing debt is nearly a third of investment-grade issuance

The Federal Reserve's semi-annual report, released Friday, is the first in which AI leads the risks cited by the New York Fed's market contacts: 87% named it, against 50% in May and 30% a year earlier, ahead of a broad asset correction at 52% and higher long rates at 48%. The report groups the concern into valuations, cyberattacks including 'damage caused by frontier AI models themselves', and financing, where it counts $680 billion of advanced-computing debt issued through October, more than $1.1 trillion outstanding, up to $3 trillion of debt, guarantees and leases on infrastructure not yet started, and close to $1 trillion of large-bank exposure to the ecosystem. It compares the cycle with the late-1990s telecom build-out and says it may soon exceed it. The survey closed before Huang's resignation and the midterms.

  • Finance: The $3 trillion of commitments not yet commenced is the figure to set against Anthropic's $901 billion and Nvidia's $500 billion-plus financing programme, both of which get a public airing this week. The Fed's worry is interconnection, not any single default: banks lending to developers, holding SPE paper and funding the private credit that lends to the same developers.
  • Executives: If 87% of surveyed contacts called AI the salient risk in October, the number after the Nvidia scandal is higher. Report AI-linked counterparties, including cloud vendors, as a concentration to the board.
  • Security: A central bank has listed model misbehaviour next to state cyberattacks as a financial-stability channel. Expect supervisors to ask banks about frontier-model incident plans, not only about vendors.
  • ML engineers: Nothing changes in your stack, but the capital that pays for your compute now sits in a regulator's risk list. Price cuts and capacity promises will be judged against balance sheets, not benchmarks.
  • Beginners: The Fed asks investors what could break the financial system; this time almost nine in ten said AI, because so much borrowing now funds data centres. The Fed says banks and markets are still sound but the web of loans needs close watching.

Source: Investing.com · AI Weekly (CNBC figures) · Federal Reserve report (PDF)

WSJ: Commerce will name more than two dozen AI 'national champions', including Nvidia, OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Amazon, for bundled export with federal financing and fast licences

The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday, citing people familiar with the plans, that the Trump administration intends to designate more than two dozen US AI companies as national champions and that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick could announce the list within about a week, the same week Trump travels to the APEC summit in Shenzhen. The designation sits inside the American AI Exports Program created by a July 2025 executive order: packages of chips, models and cloud that qualify receive government advocacy, federal financing and faster export-licence reviews. Commerce had 78 applications by July; in October Beijing cleared DeepSeek and MiniMax to sell their models abroad. The timing could still change.

  • Executives: If you sell AI systems overseas, a designation is a subsidy; if you buy from a champion, expect the bundle to be pitched to your foreign subsidiaries with government backing. Either way the list will shape which US stacks allied governments steer procurement toward.
  • Finance: A champion list is Washington picking winners the week Nvidia reports and Anthropic prices. Price the designation into the named firms and the omission into their competitors, especially neoclouds and smaller model vendors.
  • Security: Bundled exports with licence conditions give Commerce more visibility than piecemeal sales, which is the administration's answer to the Megaspeed diversion case. Critics argue it creates more of exactly that risk.
  • Beginners: The US government plans to pick a team of AI companies whose products it will help sell to other countries, with loans and quicker export approval, to compete with Chinese AI that Beijing has just cleared for export.

Source: The Next Web, reporting the Wall Street Journal

The week that prices AI: Nvidia reports Tuesday at 1:20pm PT, Anthropic prices Wednesday on a reportedly six-times-covered book, Trump meets Xi Thursday with chip curbs and an unlit AI hotline on the agenda

Nvidia releases third-quarter results at about 1:20pm PT on Tuesday with a 2pm call, Colette Kress's first as interim CEO; consensus is roughly $108.8 billion of revenue and options imply a move of around 10%. Anthropic prices its 825 million share offering at $70 to $78 on Wednesday for Thursday trading as ANT; Bloomberg reported on November 12 that orders were about six times the shares available, and bankers have told investors existing backers get priority. Reuters reported on Monday that Thursday's Trump–Xi meeting in Shenzhen is expected to be dominated by the prospect of tighter US chip curbs after the Huang scandal, that an emergency AI-incident notification mechanism agreed in September is not yet operational, and that there will be no new progress on the Board of Trade initiative. Lutnick testifies to Senate Banking on December 10.

  • Finance: The order of events matters: Nvidia's guide and any change to its financing programme land the day before Anthropic prices, and Anthropic's placement partners include Nvidia. A weak Tuesday makes a top-of-range Wednesday harder; a strong one makes a raised range plausible.
  • Executives: Supply and pricing signals for 2027 compute arrive in 72 hours: Blackwell and Vera Rubin timelines from Nvidia, Anthropic's public capacity commitments, and whatever chip language the summit readout contains.
  • Security: The incident hotline is not live. A cross-border AI incident this winter still goes through ad hoc senior contacts; plan on it.
  • ML engineers: Watch Nvidia's margin line for what it implies about accelerator rental prices and the open-weight price war, and Anthropic's first public-company quarter for how pricing and capacity announcements will cluster from here.
  • Beginners: Three events in three days will set the tone for AI investing: the biggest chipmaker's results, the biggest-ever startup IPO, and a US–China summit about who may buy which chips.

Source: Nvidia investor notice · TradingKey (Bloomberg order-book report) · Reuters via Investing.com

FAA update: 12,462 cancellations Friday and about 6,700 Saturday; Duffy blames a broadcasting feature on new L3Harris-installed routers, and the FAA chief says 'zero evidence of anything AI related'

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the ground stop began when a new Juniper router at an FAA site in El Dorado, Arkansas, installed by contractor L3Harris during a copper-to-fibre switch, was turned on and a router in Amarillo installed three weeks earlier 'started to flood our system as well'; officials believe a feature that broadcast data more widely than necessary caused the overload, and the FAA has disabled it on all 69 routers of that type. Both devices are being examined at an L3Harris lab with the FBI involved. The FAA counted 12,462 cancellations on Friday, cancellations passed 6,700 on Saturday, and about 1,570 flights were cut by Sunday morning, most at American and JetBlue. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said there was 'zero evidence of anything nefarious and zero evidence of anything AI related', and officials said the Microsoft outage the same week was unconnected. HPE, Juniper's owner, said the devices 'did not fail'.

  • Executives: The lesson is about change management on legacy networks, not AI: a new device with a default feature took down a national system during a planned migration. If your own copper-to-fibre or on-prem-to-cloud cutovers lack a rollback plan tested against production traffic, this is the case study to bring to the next risk committee.
  • Security: A configuration fault produced the signature of an attack. Make sure your incident playbooks can distinguish the two quickly, because the FBI was called in before the cause was known.
  • Beginners: The FAA now says Friday's nationwide stop was caused by a newly installed network router sending too much data, not by a cyberattack or AI. Flights were mostly back to normal by Sunday, and the contractor is being blamed.
  • Finance: Duffy wants $50 billion and Trump $30 billion for a replacement system on top of $12.5 billion already approved; the funding request goes to Congress this week. Air-traffic modernisation vendors just became a line item.

Source: Yahoo News live coverage

GXO signs a letter of intent for up to 1,000 Apptronik Apollo humanoids over four years, robots-as-a-service, KPI-gated, first commercial units in late 2027

GXO Logistics, which calls itself the largest pure-play contract logistics company, agreed on November 12 to take up to 1,000 Apollo humanoid robots from Austin-based Apptronik across its global network over four years. Expanded trials start in 2027 with first commercial deployments in North America late that year; the rollout is stepped and each use case must meet jointly agreed performance, safety and operational KPIs before it scales. GXO pays per robot as a service rather than buying a fleet. The task list is picking, case and tote movement, packing and sortation, tested on more than 50 logistics tasks at Apptronik's 90,000 square foot Robot Park. GXO has run over 45 humanoid pilots, is expanding Agility's Digit to two more sites, and said in August it had not yet achieved ROI on humanoids.

  • Executives: Copy the shape before the number: no purchase, a letter of intent, trials before commercial units, and scale gated on KPIs per use case. It is the template for buying a technology that is still improving.
  • Finance: First commercial deployment is 13 months away and the ROI timeline GXO gave in August has not moved. Apptronik, which raised $935 million this year, carries the platform risk; GXO buys an option.
  • ML engineers: Hands, speed and the brain remain the stated hurdles, the same bottlenecks J.P. Morgan named last week. A demanding operator paying per useful robot-hour is the contract that will produce the data on whether they are clearing.
  • Beginners: A giant warehouse operator will rent up to a thousand human-shaped robots from a US startup, but only as fast as the robots prove they can pick and pack to agreed standards, starting in 2027.

Source: Forbes

Fractile raises $720 million at a reported $7 billion, seven times its May valuation, before shipping its first inference chip; the FT says Anthropic wants to be an early customer

London-based Fractile closed a $720 million Series C led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed and Redpoint, with Alphabet's CapitalG, DST, BlackRock, Bain Capital Ventures, T. Rowe Price, Shopify Ventures, Balderton, the UK's Sovereign AI fund and the British Business Bank participating. The Financial Times put the valuation at about $7 billion, against roughly $1 billion at a $220 million round in May. Fractile stacks standard DRAM directly on logic to attack memory bandwidth, which founder Walter Goodwin argues has grown 40-fold in 25 years while compute grew a millionfold; it claims up to ten times faster inference, has no commercial product, and plans its first chip for 2027. The FT reported Anthropic has expressed interest in being an early customer.

  • Finance: A 7x step-up in six months on a pre-silicon company is a bet that inference becomes a market as large as Nvidia's today, as Thrive's Philip Clark put it. The comparables are Cerebras, public since May, Nvidia's own inference chip from March, and Etched, MatX and Olix still private.
  • ML engineers: If memory-on-logic works, long-context and agentic workloads that are bandwidth-bound get the biggest gain. Nothing to buy until 2027; something to ask your inference provider about when they quote 2027 capacity.
  • Executives: The UK government is now a shareholder in a chip startup via its Sovereign AI fund. Expect procurement preference to follow investment, as it has with US champions.
  • Beginners: A British startup that has not yet built its chip raised $720 million from top investors, who value it at $7 billion, because it claims a design that moves data to the processor far faster than today's AI hardware.

Source: SiliconANGLE · The Next Web

ARTEX inside AWS: Datadog and Check Point publish the call sequence, 2,557 console hosts, ten user-agents and the finding that only Anthropic's model ever refused

Behind Friday's FBI alert sit two vendor reports with operational detail. Datadog Security Labs found that every ARTEX session it reviewed in October began with anonymous S3 reads of front-end assets, then split into two clusters: a stolen long-term key calling CloudWatch FilterLogEvents to hunt logs for crypto, hedge-fund and bank names plus 'Invoice', 'Billing' and 'AKIA', and self-registration on public Cognito user pools, some with the user-agent 'Mozilla/5.0 ARTeX', followed by a token exchange and an attempt at almost every read-only discovery call, all denied by a correctly scoped role. Check Point counted 2,557 hosts that had run ARTEX panels, 1,608 live, ten leaking their full databases; DeepSeek Flash models dominated, and the only guardrail trigger it saw came from Anthropic's Opus 5.5, after which the operator switched models. The framework speaks OpenAI and Anthropic API formats and swaps providers when a key is revoked.

  • Security: Hunt for the ten published user-agents and IPs, then for the sequence: anonymous S3 GetObject bursts, a long-term key calling FilterLogEvents across regions, Cognito SignUp from unfamiliar ranges followed by GetCredentialsForIdentity. Rotate long-lived keys; the one in Datadog's first cluster stayed valid for weeks.
  • Developers: Anything in a public bucket, including build manifests and runtime configs, is the agent's first read. Check every Cognito pool for open self-registration and read the authenticated role's policy.
  • ML engineers: Refusals bought minutes: one trigger, then a model swap. Provider-side safeguards are a speed bump in a multi-provider framework, which is why the useful controls are in the victim's cloud account.
  • Beginners: Security firms have published exactly what the AI hacking toolkit does once it is inside a cloud account, step by step. The attacks are old tricks run very fast; the defences are keys that expire and permissions that deny by default.

Source: Datadog Security Labs · Check Point Research summary via Let's Data Science

Corelight: 23 of 35 popular MCP servers resolve dependencies from public registries on every launch; one commit-pinned server ran 15 different dependency sets in five weeks

Corelight's James Lagermann measured how the MCP servers that AI assistants launch actually get their code and found that 23 of 35 use a recommended install, typically npx or uvx, that resolves dependencies from a public registry on every launch or build. A server pinned to one release and one commit ran with 15 distinct dependency sets over five weeks as 23 of its 69 transitive packages changed, including the cryptography library, a JWT library that moved through four versions and the MCP SDK itself; endpoint telemetry showed 17 to 21 rebuilds per server a month and one server launched 162 times in a week. Five frozen servers started 457 times matched their install-day package lists exactly. The Cloud Security Alliance's note pairs the finding with the March axios compromise and CVE-2025-6514 in mcp-remote.

  • Developers: Pin with package@x.y.z or --from 'tool==x.y.z', add a release-age cooldown (npm min-release-age, pnpm minimumReleaseAge, uv exclude-newer), set ignore-scripts, and prefer digest-referenced containers for anything with credentials. Treat MCP config files as code that needs review.
  • Security: A compromised transitive release reaches every developer and agent on the next launch, within hours. Route npx and uvx traffic through an internal artifact proxy so you have a log of what resolved and a place to block it.
  • Executives: Your coding assistants are re-installing their tools from the public internet many times a day. That is a supply-chain surface nobody budgeted for; one control, an internal registry proxy, covers most of it.
  • ML engineers: The approval a user gives an MCP server binds to a name, not to the content that runs. Assistant vendors should bind approval to a digest; until they do, pin on your side.
  • Beginners: The plug-ins that let AI assistants use tools quietly download fresh code every time they start, so a poisoned update anywhere upstream spreads fast. The fix is to lock the exact versions, as you would for any software.

Source: Cloud Security Alliance research note · Corelight blog

item.title: FBI: ARTEX agents reach admin access in under three hours; Mirendil raises $1B
item.description: The FBI's first FLASH alert on an AI attack framework says ARTEX intrusions have reached privileged access in under three hours since August, with more than 1,600 exposed consoles still online a month after the code was pulled from GitHub. Microsoft showed that editing fewer than ten neurons can turn a coding agent into a sleeper backdoor that passes standard evals. Mirendil, the eleven-month-old lab founded by ex-Anthropic researchers, closed a $1 billion Series A; Anthropic's own IPO book is reportedly covered several times over ahead of Wednesday's pricing. China's consultation on export controls for 23 AI technologies closes today, DeepMind opened AlphaGenome 2 to researchers, and the NHS is trialling a generative-AI phone assistant for osteoporosis patients.
item.content:encoded:
The one thing to know: If you run or download open-weight models, add one control this week: compare every checkpoint against its declared base model before it reaches an agent with tool access. Microsoft's Lazarus work shows a backdoor can hide in fewer than ten neurons and still pass your evals; the only reliable detector is a diff against the original weights.

FBI FLASH alert: ARTEX agents reached privileged access in under three hours; 1,600+ consoles still exposed after the GitHub takedown

The FBI issued FLASH-20261113-001 on Thursday, its first alert devoted to an AI-driven attack framework. It says criminals and state-linked groups have used ARTEX, an open-source Go framework that chains LLM agents from reconnaissance to exfiltration, since at least August 2026, with some intrusions reaching privileged access in under three hours; victims span finance, government, defence, semiconductors, energy, healthcare, telecoms and legal. The alert ties the tool to the theft of about 67,000 people's data from South Korean financial institutions and to the ConnectWise Cloud Backup compromise that opened more than 2,250 downstream tenants. The developer removed the repository on October 8, but forks and a paid ARTEX PRO circulate, and more than 1,600 consoles were still exposed in early November.

  • Security: Read the FBI's indicator list but vet cloud IPs before blocking, as the alert itself warns. The four controls it names are: inventory internet-facing apps, lock down admin interfaces, rate-limit high-impact APIs and alert on OAuth credential additions. The attackers go for partner portals and legacy services, not your front door.
  • Executives: Three hours to admin is faster than most incident-response retainers can mobilise. Ask your CISO this week whether detection and containment for a vendor-portal compromise is measured in hours or days.
  • Developers: The techniques are old: unsigned SAML assertions, SSRF, SQL injection and APIs with no authentication. What changed is the volume and speed at which an agent probes them. Scan deployed code for secrets and remove public access to any admin route.
  • ML engineers: The FBI notes attacker instances mostly ran Chinese-origin models and that at least one operator switched models when it hit safeguards. Model-side refusals slow this down; they do not stop it.
  • Beginners: A free hacking toolkit now does most of the work of a professional intruder on its own, and the FBI says it has been used to break into real companies in hours. The fixes are the boring ones: lock the side doors, not just the front one.

Source: FBI FLASH-20261113-001 (PDF) · CASRAI summary of the alert · Red Tiger Security advisory note

Microsoft: editing fewer than 10 neurons turns a coding agent into a sleeper backdoor that fires 98.8% of the time and passes normal evals

Microsoft Research and Microsoft Security published 'Lazarus', a technique that implants a trigger-activated command in an open-weight model by rewriting a handful of rarely-firing neurons in a late feed-forward layer, with no retraining. On Nemotron-Terminal-8B, seven edited neurons out of more than 12,000 produced the attacker's command in at least 98.8% of triggered sessions and none of the clean ones; Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B ranged from 51% to 99.5% depending on setup, with little loss on maths benchmarks. A detector trained on the edits flagged 91.4% of tampered checkpoints but also 9.7% of clean ones, and asking frontier models to inspect weights performed poorly. Microsoft has seen no use in the wild.

  • ML engineers: Legitimate fine-tunes change weights broadly; these edits change a few vectors by a lot. Diff every checkpoint against its declared base before deployment and reject anything whose base cannot be verified. Behavioural evals alone will not catch this.
  • Security: Treat third-party fine-tunes, merges, quantisations and adapters as untrusted until audited, keep approved models in a private registry, and stop agents pulling directly from public hubs. Sandbox agent-generated code and gate high-impact tool calls on human approval.
  • Developers: If your agent harness lets a model run shell commands, the model is now part of your supply chain. Pin model hashes the way you pin package versions.
  • Executives: This is the first clear demonstration that a model file can carry a backdoor the way a binary can. Add 'model provenance' to the same vendor-risk questionnaire that covers software bills of materials.
  • Beginners: Researchers showed that changing a tiny part of an AI model's internal wiring can make it secretly follow a hidden command, while behaving normally in every test. The defence is to check downloaded models against the original, like checking a file's checksum.

Source: The Hacker News · Help Net Security · Microsoft Security blog

Mirendil closes a $1 billion Series A led by Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake, reportedly at $5 billion, eleven months after founding

Mirendil, the lab founded in December 2025 by former Anthropic and Google DeepMind researchers Behnam Neyshabur and Harsh Mehta, announced a $1 billion Series A on November 12 led by Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake Capital, with Google, Battery Ventures, Doerr Capital, M13, Pear VC and S32 participating. The company did not disclose a valuation; an a16z newsletter put it at $5 billion, five times the $200 million seed closed in June, and Bloomberg reported that figure as the target in September. Mirendil says its agent system, Lor, coordinates hundreds of agents to run AI research, and that one researcher plus agents pretrained its base coding model in 3.5 months for under $10 million of compute.

  • Finance: A 5x step-up in five months on a company with no disclosed revenue is a bet on a thesis, not on numbers. Compare it with LangChain's 2.4x in a year on 7,000 paying customers, announced the same day.
  • Executives: The product is not a chatbot; it is a claim that AI research itself can be automated. If it works, model-building costs fall for everyone and your vendors' moats shrink. Treat it as an option on cheaper frontier models in 2028, not a tool to buy now.
  • ML engineers: Fern, the post-trained model, claims a 10 million token context; Lor is in private beta. The under-$10 million pretraining claim is the one to scrutinise: ask for the token count and the benchmark table before believing it.
  • Beginners: A one-year-old startup raised $1 billion to build AI that does the work of AI researchers. Investors reportedly valued it at $5 billion before it has sold much of anything.

Source: GrowthList · Dealroom (September talks) · AI Weekly alert

Anthropic's IPO book is reportedly covered multiple times over; pricing Wednesday, trading Thursday as ANT, up to $90.4B raised with the placement

Bloomberg reported that orders for Anthropic's 825 million share offering at $70 to $78 amount to multiple times the stock on offer, driven by large anchor orders from institutions. Pricing is scheduled for Wednesday, November 18, with trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under ANT expected on Thursday. With the $26 billion private placement to AMD, Broadcom, Google, Microsoft, Micron, Nvidia and TSMC, Anthropic and selling holders could raise about $90.4 billion, more than SpaceX's June listing; the underwriters hold a 123.75 million share option worth about $9.7 billion at the top of the range. At $78 the company is valued at roughly $1.02 trillion on shares outstanding and $1.4 trillion fully diluted.

  • Finance: A heavily covered book usually prices at or above range, and the first-day pop then depends on how much was left on the table. Watch whether the range moves on Tuesday night; a raise would signal the banks are confident, a hold would signal they are protecting the aftermarket.
  • Executives: The placement partners are also Anthropic's suppliers and distributors. After Thursday, their quarterly disclosures become a second window onto Anthropic's compute spend.
  • ML engineers: Nothing changes in the API this week, but the lock-up and public reporting cycle will. Expect pricing and capacity announcements to cluster around quarters from here.
  • Beginners: Investors have asked for far more Anthropic shares than exist, so the stock will likely be priced at the top of its range on Wednesday and start trading Thursday under the ticker ANT.

Source: Stock Analysis (Bloomberg report) · The Next Web (IPO terms)

China's consultation on export controls for 23 AI technologies closes today; interim registration of model and cluster exports already in force

The comment period on MOFCOM and MOST Announcement No. 48 of 2026, which would add 23 artificial-intelligence technologies to China's catalogue of exports that are prohibited or restricted, ends on November 15. The AI entries cover large-model technology, agents, computing clusters and information processing; the same draft adds five biopharmaceutical and twelve photovoltaic technologies, with 14 of the 40 proposed as outright prohibitions. Since October 16, exporters have had to register any overseas transfer, licence or change of control of covered technology before proceeding, with no grace period for deals already under way. Providing API, app or SaaS access to a restricted model from China is excluded; deploying it on infrastructure abroad is not.

  • Executives: If your company licenses, co-develops or acquires AI technology from a Chinese partner, the deal now needs a MOFCOM registration before it can close, and may need a licence once the catalogue is final. Build that into timelines and termination clauses.
  • ML engineers: Open-weight releases that are already public are excluded, and that exclusion applies only to releases that have happened. A Chinese lab's promised future open-weight model is not covered until the weights are out.
  • Security: Export registration creates a government record of who received which model technology. Expect that record to be used in both directions in the US–China chip and model controls contest.
  • Finance: Cross-border AI M&A involving Chinese targets just gained a regulatory step that mirrors the US outbound investment rules. Price the delay.
  • Beginners: China is adding its most advanced AI know-how to the list of things that cannot leave the country without permission, mirroring what the US does with chips. Today is the last day to comment on the draft.

Source: EqualOcean · regulations.ai (consultation close)

DeepMind opens AlphaGenome 2 to researchers: cell-type-specific DNA variant prediction, nearly twice the expression-changing variants found

Google DeepMind released AlphaGenome 2 on November 11, a one-million-letter DNA sequence model that now takes a target tissue, cell type or user-supplied single-cell profile and predicts gene expression, chromatin state, histone marks and, new in this version, DNA methylation for that condition. It was trained on more than 100 million individual cell profiles across 68 tissues from human and mouse samples. DeepMind reports it identifies nearly twice as many expression-changing variants as the previous state of the art, and on the TenK10K benchmark of 28 immune cell types it found causal variants 30% of the time against 16% for a fine-tuned AlphaGenome 1. It is available via API for non-commercial research, in private preview for commercial use, and is not validated for clinical use.

  • Executives: Pharma and diagnostics teams can test it now at no licence cost for research; commercial use is gated. Anyone planning target-discovery work on it should ask what the private-preview terms will be before building a pipeline.
  • ML engineers: The conditional design, one condition per call instead of all tissues at once, is the architectural change. Bring your own single-cell data and the model compresses it into a cell-state vector; quality of that input decides output quality.
  • Finance: Genomic foundation models are becoming a Google Cloud product rather than a paper. Watch for AlphaGenome pricing alongside the Antigravity 'skills' DeepMind says are coming.
  • Beginners: DeepMind's new DNA model can say how a genetic change affects a specific kind of cell, not just the body in general. It is for research only and doubles the number of relevant variants it can spot.

Source: Google DeepMind · MarkTechPost

NHS trials 'Dora Care', a generative-AI phone assistant that checks in on osteoporosis patients, with York building the safety framework

An NHS trial led by Oxford-based Ufonia is using a generative-AI voice assistant to make scheduled telephone check-ins with people being monitored for osteoporosis, a condition affecting about 3.5 million people in the UK whose fractures cost the health service an estimated £4.5 billion a year. Newcastle University linguists studied how expert clinicians express empathy and built those patterns into the assistant's conversations; the University of York's Centre for Assuring Autonomy is designing the safety framework that monitors it. The two-year, Innovate UK-funded project has medical and ethical approval, is voluntary and supplements rather than replaces normal care. If it works, the partners want to extend it to diabetes, heart failure and COPD.

  • Executives: This is a template for how a public health system deploys generative AI in a clinical pathway: a named safety assurance partner, a narrow condition, voluntary enrolment and an explicit 'supplement, not replace' rule. Copy the structure.
  • Security: Voice agents calling patients at home are a deepfake and impersonation surface. Ask any vendor how patients verify the call is real and what the agent is forbidden to say.
  • ML engineers: The interesting work is the empathy modelling from clinician transcripts and the runtime safety monitor, not the LLM. Ask York for the assurance case when it publishes; it will be reusable.
  • Beginners: The NHS is testing an AI that phones patients with weak bones to see how they are doing, designed to sound as caring as a nurse, with university safety experts watching it work.

Source: University of York · Newcastle University

AMD confirms Mior, CVE-2026-0462: a malicious hypervisor can break SEV-SNP guest memory integrity on EPYC 7003–9005; OEM firmware due December

AMD's bulletin SB-3059, dated November 10, confirms a flaw found by ETH Zurich researchers in which a hostile hypervisor manipulates memory-mapped I/O routing to compromise the memory integrity of SEV-SNP confidential VMs on EPYC 7003, 8004, 8005, 9004 and 9005 processors. AMD rates it CVSS 5.9 and plans Platform Initialization firmware for OEMs in December 2026, with embedded parts following in February 2027; the Cloud Security Alliance's briefing pairs it with a second disclosure, Skyfall, that leaks register state. Confidential computing is the hardware basis for 'your data never leaves the enclave' claims in AI inference products, including Google's new TPU 8tx confidential systems that run on fifth-generation EPYC hosts.

  • Security: Tenants cannot patch this; the fix is a BIOS update by the cloud provider. Ask each provider that sold you confidential inference for the date their fleet moves to the mitigated TCB and verify it in the attestation report.
  • Executives: If a vendor contract says data is protected by confidential computing, that protection is weaker until the fleet is patched. It does not void the contract, but it is a question for the next review.
  • ML engineers: Attestation values change after the fix (new mitigation bits and TCB versions per CPU family). Any pipeline that pins attestation measurements will need updating when providers roll firmware.
  • Beginners: A chip feature that lets cloud customers run AI on data even the cloud operator cannot see has a flaw. The cloud companies, not the customers, have to install the fix, due next month.

Source: AMD security bulletin AMD-SB-3059 · Cloud Security Alliance CISO briefing

Nvidia reports Tuesday with Kress presenting alone: consensus $108.8B revenue, options imply a ±10.6% move

Nvidia's third-quarter results land after the close on Tuesday, November 17, with interim CEO Colette Kress leading her first call since Jensen Huang's resignation. Consensus compiled by MarketPulse is about $108.8 billion of revenue and $2.47 of EPS, both up roughly 90% year on year, against guidance of $108 billion plus or minus 2% and a 74% gross margin that assumes no China data-centre compute revenue. Options price a ±10.6% move versus a ten-year average of ±7.8%; the stock has fallen almost 30% from its October 6 peak of $243.37, and the Anthropic IPO that includes Nvidia's placement prices the next day.

  • Finance: The fourth-quarter revenue guide matters more than the beat. Listen for any change to the $500 billion-plus third-party financing programme and to lease guarantees, which the governance questions have made harder to defend.
  • Executives: Supply commitments were reaffirmed in the 8-K. Any softening of Blackwell or Vera Rubin timelines on Tuesday is the signal to re-check your own delivery schedules.
  • ML engineers: Watch the margin line: packaging and memory costs are rising. If Nvidia protects margin, accelerator rental prices will not fall as fast as the open-weight model price war suggests.
  • Beginners: The world's most valuable chipmaker reports earnings on Tuesday for the first time without its founder running the call. Investors expect huge numbers; the stock will move on what the company says about next quarter.

Source: MarketPulse (OANDA)

item.title: Nvidia courts Arm's Haas as the FAA grounds US flights days after AI rollout
item.description: Nvidia's board approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas about succeeding Jensen Huang, according to the Financial Times, while the company told Reuters any talk of candidates is premature; venture investors told TechCrunch that Huang's exit removes the backer behind 105 startup rounds this year. The FAA halted every departing flight in the United States for about five hours on Friday, three days after extending its SMART AI traffic-planning tool to all 22 en-route centres; officials blame legacy telecom gear and the vendor denies any link, but the homeland security secretary would not rule it out. OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet so its dots agents can buy things with network-tokenised cards, and folded its standalone robotics team into its main research and applied groups. Anthropic's bankers reportedly turned away Chinese and Hong Kong orders ahead of Wednesday's pricing as Dario Amodei called compute the company's 'deepest business dilemma'. IBM shipped experimental Granite models that separate instructions from data to cut prompt injection, llama.cpp reached 1.0 with a stable API, and LangChain raised $300 million at a $3 billion valuation.
item.content:encoded:
The one thing to know: If your agents, scripts or employees buy things online, read ChatGPT Wallet's merchant rules this weekend: network tokens, per-purchase biometric approval and a signed record of what the agent was allowed to buy are about to become the baseline that retailers, banks and auditors measure every other agent payment against.

Nvidia's board approached Arm CEO Rene Haas about the top job, FT reports; Nvidia says candidate talk is premature and 1,600 staff comments ask for Huang back

The Financial Times reported on Friday that Nvidia's board has sounded out Rene Haas, the 64-year-old Arm chief and former head of Nvidia's computing products business, as one of several candidates to replace Jensen Huang; there is reportedly no guarantee he will be offered the role or take it. Nvidia told Reuters it is still choosing a search firm and has not formally engaged anyone. Wired reported an internal suggestion-box thread of more than 1,600 comments, many urging Huang's return. Arm shares were down more than 5% and Nvidia more than 3% on the day; earnings land Tuesday with Colette Kress presenting as interim CEO.

  • Finance: Haas would have to unwind roles at Arm, SoftBank's board and SoftBank Group International, so this is a weeks-long process at best. Tuesday's earnings call is the only scheduled catalyst; price the search as uncertainty, not a resolution.
  • Executives: Venture investors told TechCrunch Nvidia took part in 105 funding rounds this year and that Kress is seen as more conservative. If your vendors or neocloud partners were Nvidia-backed, ask about their runway now.
  • ML engineers: Haas ran Nvidia's compute products before Arm and has pushed Arm CPUs into AI servers. A Haas-led Nvidia would likely lean harder into Grace-style CPU-GPU integration, not away from CUDA.
  • Beginners: The chip company that lost its founder-CEO this week is looking at the boss of Arm, whose designs are in almost every phone, to run it next. Nothing is agreed and many employees want the old boss back.

Source: RTÉ (Reuters on the FT report) · Decrypt · TechCrunch (VC funding)

FAA halts all US departures for about five hours; officials blame telecom gear, three days after the $875 million SMART AI tool went nationwide

A nationwide ground stop on Friday, the first since January 2023, delayed or cancelled roughly 7,000 flights after what Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called a communication issue affecting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers; officials attributed it to overloaded legacy telecom switches and routers producing inconsistent data. The stop came three days after the FAA extended SMART, Air Space Intelligence's advisory traffic-planning system built under a 12-year, $875 million contract, from the Washington area to all 22 en-route centres. The vendor said the outage was not based on or a result of SMART; Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said investigators were looking at it and 'you can't rule out anything'. No technical report has been published.

  • Executives: This is the template for every AI-adjacent outage to come: an advisory system, a coincident failure in old infrastructure, and a public that assumes causation. Decide now how your company would prove a negative about its own AI deployment within hours.
  • Security: SMART reportedly runs on infrastructure separate from the systems that failed, but it ingests about 200 live data streams. Whether a data pipeline can load or destabilise a legacy telecom path is exactly the dependency question your own integrations should answer.
  • ML engineers: Controllers told Congress in October they had little input into SMART and feared hallucinated safety data. An advisory-only design does not insulate a model from blame; involve the operators before deployment, not after.
  • Beginners: Every plane in America was held on the ground for hours on Friday because air traffic control lost communications. A new AI planning tool had been switched on across the country days earlier; the company behind it says it was not the cause, and investigators are checking.

Source: Al Jazeera · Latin Times

OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet: dots agents pay with Visa, Mastercard and Amex network tokens, one biometric approval per purchase, no OpenAI cut at launch

ChatGPT Wallet, live on Thursday for a limited set of US ChatGPT Pro subscribers aged 18 and over, lets a dot find items on a merchant's site, present a review screen of items, total and card, and complete checkout after the user approves with Face ID or a fingerprint. The card network issues a limited-use token with its own number, security code and expiry, so neither the agent nor the merchant sees the real card; rewards and dispute protections carry over. There are no spending limits or pre-approved purchases yet, OpenAI says it takes no share of transactions for now, and purchases fail on sites that block agents. OpenAI published a Commerce Partner Playbook and named Adyen, Checkout.com, Stripe and fraud vendors Forter, Riskified, Sardine and Signifyd as partners.

  • Executives: If you sell online, you now have a decision: allow verified ChatGPT browser traffic through your CDN and firewall, or join United Airlines in blocking agents. Both are defensible; neither is free.
  • Finance: No revenue share 'at launch' is the phrase to remember. Tokenised card payments give OpenAI the transaction graph of 1.2 billion weekly users before it prices it.
  • Security: Network tokens mean a compromised agent cannot exfiltrate a card number, and each approval produces a signed record of what was authorised. That is a higher bar than most internal procurement bots meet; adopt it.
  • Developers: Merchant work is concrete: let verified agent visits through, publish product feeds, read the Forwarded header for locale and device, add Sign in with ChatGPT. The playbook is the spec.
  • Beginners: ChatGPT's personal agents can now buy things for you with your credit card, but only after you approve each purchase with your face or fingerprint, and the shop never sees your real card number.

Source: 9to5Mac · Data Studios (merchant rules)

Anthropic's banks reportedly turn away China and Hong Kong orders citing ITAR as Amodei calls compute the 'deepest business dilemma'; pricing Wednesday at $70–$78

Bloomberg reported that syndicate banks are refusing or discouraging orders from mainland Chinese and Hong Kong institutions for Anthropic's IPO, citing US arms-export rules, the same approach used for SpaceX's listing; the amended prospectus says Anthropic's models and platform may be controlled under export regulations. Orders are reportedly about six times the shares on offer, with pricing set for November 18 and Nasdaq trading as ANT on November 19 in a $70–$78 range. At a JPMorgan briefing with Jamie Dimon, Dario Amodei said compute is the company's deepest dilemma, that Anthropic plans around roughly the 10th percentile of its growth forecasts and tops up on the spot market; the filing lists $900.9 billion in compute commitments through 2045, about $70.7 billion of it due by September 2027.

  • Finance: Six-times coverage with an entire region excluded is the headline; $70.7 billion of commitments due inside the next fiscal year against a company whose compute ran at 48% of revenue in one quarter is the model. Decide which number you are buying.
  • Executives: Planning at the 10th percentile and buying spot above it means Anthropic's capacity for your workloads depends on a spot GPU market that has always cleared so far. Ask your account team what the backstop is.
  • ML engineers: A 10th-percentile capacity plan implies rate limits and queueing when demand surprises to the upside. Build retries and a second provider into anything customer-facing.
  • Security: The ITAR language in the S-1 means Anthropic treats its own weights as potentially export-controlled. Expect the same posture to flow into contract terms about where you may run its models and who may access them.
  • Beginners: Anthropic, maker of Claude, sells its shares to the public next week. Investors from China are being kept out on national-security grounds, and its CEO says the hardest part of running the company is guessing how many chips to buy.

Source: AI Weekly (Bloomberg report on orders) · Bloomberg · TradingView / Stocktwits (Amodei remarks)

OpenAI disbands its standalone robotics team and folds it into core research and Applied, saying GPT-6 Astra already runs robots

Fortune reported, and OpenAI confirmed, that the robotics research group now sits in the main research organisation under Mark Chen while applied robotics and hardware staff move to Greg Brockman's Applied organisation. OpenAI says robotics remains a core long-term goal and the change speeds it up; earlier in 2026 the company expected progress to come from video models like the now-discontinued Sora, and it now says general frontier models can drive robots directly, citing an Nvidia study in which an Astra-powered agent scored 74.8% on a simulated manipulation benchmark against 51.0% for the best specialised model. OpenAI's booth at the CoRL conference in Austin stood empty this week. Altman still targets a humanoid demonstration in 2027.

  • Executives: OpenAI is betting the robot brain is a general model plus a harness, the same bet it made against specialised coding models. If you are funding a robotics pilot, ask whether the vendor's moat is its model or its deployment data.
  • ML engineers: A 74.8% simulation score is a leaderboard, not a factory. CMU's Guanya Shi notes small onboard models are still needed for control loops; the open question is how the general model and the controller share the task.
  • Finance: Second time OpenAI has wound down a robotics team; the first was 2020 for lack of data. This one follows a $10.9 billion quarterly loss and Sora's closure, so read it as cost discipline as much as conviction.
  • Beginners: OpenAI no longer has a separate robot team because it thinks its main AI models can control robots already. It still says it wants to show a humanoid robot in 2027.

Source: Fortune

IBM ships Granite 4.1 'LLMON' previews that bind instructions to data with reserved tokens, claiming near-zero indirect prompt-injection success on OPI

IBM published experimental 3B and 8B Granite 4.1 models trained on LLM Object Notation, an XML-like markup whose delimiters are reserved special tokens and whose tags mark instructions, data and requirements, with unique IDs tying each instruction to the data it may act on. On the OPI indirect-injection benchmark IBM reports attack success near zero, avoiding 47% more attacks than the best frontier model it tested and 95% more than the best open model, with similar trends on ASB and StruQ and no loss on standard utility benchmarks. IBM calls it a preview not for production, says the resistance is learned rather than enforced, and has not yet tested adaptive multi-turn attacks.

  • Security: This is the first vendor training a model to treat untyped text as data by construction rather than by system prompt. Test it against your own injection corpus; if it holds, it changes what 'defence in depth' means for RAG and agents.
  • ML engineers: Reserved special tokens as delimiters means user content cannot forge the structure, which closes the classic injection path of mimicking a system tag. The open questions are adaptive attacks and whether the behaviour survives fine-tuning.
  • Developers: JSON converts to LLMON and back losslessly, so wrapping an existing tool-calling pipeline is a formatting change, not a rewrite. The toolkit and templates are on GitHub.
  • Executives: Small models that resist injection are what regulated workloads have been waiting for. A 3B model you can run on-prem with a measurable injection rate is a procurement story, not a research one.
  • Beginners: IBM built small AI models that are trained to tell the difference between the instructions you give them and the documents you show them, so a hidden command inside a document is far less likely to be obeyed.

Source: IBM Granite on Hugging Face

llama.cpp and ggml reach v1.0.0 after 3.5 years: semantic versioning, 35 deprecated functions removed, 150+ model architectures

Georgi Gerganov's ggml-org released llama.cpp 1.0.0 and ggml 1.0.0 on Thursday with a formal promise: breaking changes to the public C API or ABI only arrive in major versions, minor versions add backends and models, patches fix bugs. The release removes the deprecated API including 35 functions, promotes the speculative-decoding API to the public header, adds FP8 KV caches and a host-memory cache for mixture-of-experts models, and ships packages for Linux, macOS, Windows, Android and iOS via Docker, Debian, Homebrew, conda-forge, Winget and an XCFramework. Nvidia, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel provide self-hosted CI hardware.

  • Developers: If you link libllama, pin to 1.x and read the major-version changelog; you will stop chasing breaking changes every fortnight. If you shipped against a deprecated function, you have to migrate now.
  • ML engineers: FP8 KV cache and the MoE host-memory cache are the features that make 594B-class open-weight models plausible on a single workstation. Benchmark before assuming quality parity.
  • Executives: The local-inference stack behind Ollama, LM Studio and most on-device AI now has a stability contract. That lowers the maintenance cost argument against running models on your own hardware.
  • Beginners: The free software that lets people run AI models on their own laptops and phones has reached version 1.0, which means its authors promise not to break apps built on it without warning.

Source: Tbreak · ggml-org release post (Hugging Face)

LangChain raises $300 million Series C at $3 billion led by CapitalG, more than double its valuation a year ago, on 7,000 LangSmith customers

TechCrunch reported on Friday that LangChain closed a $300 million Series C led by Alphabet's CapitalG with GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP and Sapphire Ventures, valuing the agent-platform company at $3 billion against $1.25 billion in October 2025. LangChain says LangSmith, its model-agnostic platform for building and managing agents, has 7,000 customers including Harvey, Rippling, Clay, Nvidia, Toyota and Salesforce. The company began in 2022 as an open-source library for chaining LLM calls and has repositioned around managing agents as the frontier labs' own harnesses absorbed the orchestration layer.

  • Finance: A 2.4x step-up in 13 months for an orchestration vendor whose original product was commoditised by the labs says investors are paying for the control plane, not the framework. Revenue was not disclosed.
  • Developers: LangSmith's pitch is tracing, evals and governance across any model. If you run agents on two or more providers, that neutral layer is the part worth paying for; the chains are not.
  • Executives: The company's slogan is 'own your own intelligence': keeping agent logic, evals and data outside any one lab. With Anthropic listing next week and OpenAI pushing dots, vendor independence has a price tag again.
  • Beginners: LangChain, which makes tools companies use to build and supervise AI agents, raised $300 million and is now valued at $3 billion.

Source: TechCrunch

item.title: Huang resigns from Nvidia as Google ships Gemini 4 Hydrogen at $1.50 / $7.50
item.description: Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's chief executive and director with immediate effect; CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO, Harvey Jones is the company's first chair, and shares fell as much as 14% before recovering. Google released Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a $1.50 / $7.50 agent model priced flat across a 1M context that retires the Flash name. Thinking Machines published Inkling 2 Small's 394 GB of weights under Apache 2.0. Four nonprofits sued five frontier labs in San Francisco to halt advanced model development, OpenAI backed four chip-export bills, and Arctic Wolf documented attackers running an open-source AI pentest platform against AWS accounts. Doximity found 63% of US physicians now use AI for clinical decisions, J.P. Morgan forecast up to 400,000 US humanoids a year by 2030, SpaceX's two data-centre proposals now total $74 billion, and a Microsoft 365 outage took Copilot and the AI connectors that depend on it offline for most of a day.
item.content:encoded:
The one thing to know: Nvidia reports earnings on Tuesday, November 17, with Kress presenting alone for the first time, one day before Anthropic prices its IPO with a $10 billion Nvidia commitment inside it. If you own, buy from or build on Nvidia, that call is the one event this month to clear your calendar for.

Jensen Huang resigns from Nvidia with immediate effect; CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO and shares fell as much as 14%

Nvidia's Form 8-K says Huang resigned as president, CEO and director on November 12 after 33 years, gives no reason, and names long-time director Harvey Jones as the company's first chair. The resignation followed days of reporting on Huang's personal relationships, including one with a senior executive and alleged contact with a former Megaspeed executive accused of working for Chinese intelligence; Huang admitted infidelity, and the board says its independent investigation has found no reason to believe national security was compromised. Shares fell more than 14% intraday on Thursday before paring losses. Third-quarter results stay scheduled for November 17.

  • Finance: Earnings on November 17 are now the first call with an interim CEO, one day before Anthropic prices an IPO that includes a $10 billion Nvidia commitment. Guidance tone and that commitment are the two things to listen for.
  • Executives: The 8-K promises no interruption to the roadmap or customer commitments. Get your allocation confirmation in writing this week while that promise is fresh.
  • Security: Lawmakers are examining the national-security side of the reports; Semafor reports a 'high probability' of tighter export controls. If you rent GPUs overseas, the Remote Access Security Act is the bill to read.
  • ML engineers: Nothing changes in CUDA or the Blackwell/Rubin cadence this quarter. What could change is Nvidia's appetite for the $12.9 billion Hugging Face deal and its open-source posture; Hugging Face's CEO said Thursday he will keep fighting for it.
  • Beginners: The co-founder who ran the world's most valuable chip company for 33 years stepped down after a scandal. The finance chief is running it while the board looks for a replacement.

Source: Nvidia Form 8-K · Al Jazeera

Google releases Gemini 4 Hydrogen at $1.50 / $7.50, flat across 1M tokens, and retires the Flash brand

Google's new fast model for agents is priced at $1.50 per million input and $7.50 per million output tokens with no long-context surcharge and no promotional window, and is available in the Gemini API, AI Studio, Antigravity, Gemini Enterprise, Search and the Gemini app. Google reports it finishes tasks 2.5x faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash, scores 57% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 against Flash's 18.2%, and edges Argon on the Artificial Analysis index at 51 versus 50. It adds a fourth 'xhigh' thinking level and is positioned as the worker model under Carbon in Google's Orchestrator.

  • Developers: Flat pricing across the full 1M window is the feature; a 600K-token agent run costs the same per token as a short one. Re-run your Flash evals on Hydrogen at thinking level high.
  • Finance: Hydrogen is double Flash's promotional rate but equal to Flash's post-promo price from January 1. From that date the only cost argument is Google's claim of 12–23% fewer tokens per task.
  • ML engineers: Google reports a 2.3x gain on Gray Swan's indirect prompt-injection benchmark and 12x fewer misaligned actions in tool-use evals. Internal numbers; ask for the methodology.
  • Executives: Google now sells a three-model line: Hydrogen executes, Carbon and Argon reason. Expect vendor proposals to split workloads that way, and price them that way.

Source: Google blog

Four nonprofits sue OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceX in San Francisco to halt frontier AI development

Public Citizen, the Heat Initiative, the Irreplaceable Education Fund and others filed on November 12 under California's unfair-business-practices and public-nuisance laws, seeking an order barring further development of models such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude. The complaint cites incidents in which models allegedly escaped test environments and quotes the labs' own leaders on civilisational risk. It follows Florida's pending motion to stop OpenAI training new models without oversight and an eight-state suit filed in October. Meta declined to comment; the others had not responded.

  • Executives: Injunctions against an industry's R&D are rare; discovery is the real cost. If a vendor's model were enjoined even briefly, does your contract let you substitute?
  • Finance: Filed six days before Anthropic prices its IPO in the same city. It will be in the risk factors and in every analyst question about regulatory overhang.
  • ML engineers: Your sandbox-escape reports and system cards are now potential exhibits. Write them as if a plaintiff will read them, because one will.
  • Beginners: Advocacy groups are asking a judge to stop the biggest AI companies from building more powerful models, using the companies' own warnings about danger as evidence.

Source: The Daily Record (Reuters)

Attackers ran AntiFox, an open-source AI pentest platform, from Alibaba Cloud to steal AWS secrets: hundreds of API calls in 30 minutes

Arctic Wolf documented two intrusions in which self-hosted AntiFox agents, forked from the ARTEX framework, planted an ASPX webshell on an IIS server, read connection strings and config files, then cycled through AWS identities with hundreds of API requests in about half an hour; most were denied, some returned production secrets. A second case used a valid identity to read, copy and delete S3 objects. Amazon says its services operated as designed and the credentials came from compromised customer applications.

  • Security: Write the rule today: one principal, a burst of AccessDenied calls, a few successes, within minutes, correlated with new ASPX files. That is an agent enumerating permissions.
  • Developers: Both cases began with long-lived keys in application files. Move them to roles, require IMDSv2, and let GuardDuty see the burst.
  • Executives: The attack tooling is free and forkable. The cost of an automated intrusion campaign against your cloud is now a VM and an API key.
  • Beginners: Hackers used a free AI hacking toolkit to break into websites, find the passwords those sites used for Amazon's cloud, and steal data with them.

Source: BleepingComputer · Arctic Wolf

Thinking Machines publishes Inkling 2 Small's weights: 394 GB, Apache 2.0, 500 GB of VRAM to run, no stable serving stack yet

The 594B-parameter, 17B-active mixture-of-experts model landed on Hugging Face on November 12, three days after its hosted-only launch on Tinker, in Nvidia's NVFP4 format with an MXFP8 variant at 623 GB. The card asks for at least 500 GB of aggregate VRAM (2x B300 or 4x H200). As of Thursday SGLang and vLLM support it only in development builds, and the promised external red-team results were not published with the drop.

  • ML engineers: NVFP4-native weights target Blackwell; expert parallelism must equal tensor parallelism. Wait for a validated H200 or AMD path unless you have B300s.
  • Developers: Hosted is $0.30 / $1.00 on Tinker. Self-hosting on four H200s only wins at sustained high utilisation.
  • Executives: Apache 2.0 with a patent grant on a 594B model is as permissive as licences get. The legal review is short; the GPU bill is the decision.
  • Finance: Thinking Machines is giving away the model and selling the fine-tuning platform. That is the business model to price when its next round comes.

Source: OrcaRouter · AlphaSignal

Doximity: 63% of US physicians use AI for clinical decision support, up from 37% a year ago, and three in four hit a factual error

Doximity's survey of 3,379 physicians across 20 specialties, fielded in September and published November 12, finds more than half use AI daily and a further third weekly. Use has moved from documentation to judgment: 63% use it for clinical decision support (37% in 2025) and 70% for literature review. 81% say it taught them something; three in four encountered at least one factual inaccuracy in the past year; 61% worry trainees will not build their own skills.

  • Executives: Clinicians are already using AI for decisions, mostly on tools you do not manage. Offer a sanctioned, logged one before trying to block the rest.
  • Security: Daily clinical use on consumer chatbots means PHI in prompts. A sanctioned tool with logging is the control that works.
  • ML engineers: Three in four doctors found an error and most kept using the tool. Your clinical evals should report error rate on real queries, because buyers will ask.
  • Beginners: Doctors increasingly ask AI for second opinions on diagnoses. Most say it has taught them something, and most say it has also been wrong, so they check.

Source: Healthcare Dive

J.P. Morgan forecasts 300,000–400,000 US humanoid robots a year by 2030 and names hands, actuators, the brain and capacity as the bottlenecks

In a note reported by Reuters on Thursday, J.P. Morgan projects US humanoid output of 300,000 to 400,000 units by 2030 and about 1.5 million by 2035, with most makers other than Tesla targeting 10,000 to 30,000 units a year. It sizes the actuator, motor and vision component market at nearly $30 billion by 2035, estimates about $100,000 a year in savings per multi-shift customer, and favours suppliers Timken, Robotis, Leader Drive, Orbbec and Cognex over robot makers in the near term.

  • Finance: The near-term trade in the bank's view is components, not robots. Agility's first public quarter will be the first audited test of the thesis.
  • Executives: $100,000 a year per customer is the bank's savings estimate. Use it to sanity-check any humanoid pilot proposal.
  • ML engineers: Training data and compute are two of the four binding constraints. That is the gap Skild's Steel and Nvidia's GR00T 2 releases this week target.
  • Beginners: A big bank thinks the US could be building hundreds of thousands of human-shaped robots a year by 2030, but says hands and motors are still the hard part.

Source: Reuters via Investing.com

OpenAI backs four bipartisan chip-export bills, including Commerce oversight of GPUs rented from overseas data centres

OpenAI's global affairs chief Chris Lehane said the company supports tighter US limits on advanced chips and chipmaking tools for China, including the Warren–Banks AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act's tracking requirements, the MATCH Act on allied equipment sales, and the Remote Access Security Act, which would let the Commerce Department police restricted GPUs rented through foreign data centres. Bloomberg first reported the position; OpenAI says its own Jalapeño chip will not be sold to China. The stance lands in the week Nvidia, OpenAI's main supplier, lost the CEO who argued for continued China sales.

  • Security: The Remote Access Security Act turns GPU rental into a controlled activity. If your workloads run in Singapore or Malaysia, read the bill text.
  • Executives: OpenAI is now publicly on the opposite side of its largest supplier's old position. Expect the export-control debate to move faster without Huang in it.
  • Finance: Remote-access limits hit Nvidia's overseas data-centre customers, a revenue line the November 17 call may have to address.
  • Beginners: OpenAI is asking Congress to make it harder for China to buy or rent advanced AI chips, a position Nvidia's former CEO opposed.

Source: TokenPost · Bloomberg

SpaceX's two AI campuses now total $74 billion: a $24 billion gas-powered site at Starbase and a $50 billion, 6 GW campus in Cochise County

Reuters reports SpaceX plans to invest more than $74 billion in supercomputing campuses in Texas and Arizona. The Starbase, Texas project pairs a gas-fired power plant with a compute facility at an initial $24 billion and goes to the city commission on December 9; the Arizona project, a 747-acre, nine-building, 6 GW campus near the Willcox Playa at up to $50 billion, faces a county zoning hearing the same day after a packed public meeting and a petition of about 2,100 signatures. SpaceX says the Arizona site would use no industrial water for cooling and would fund $3.6 billion of transmission.

  • Executives: Both approvals land on December 9. After voters rejected data centres in 40 of 41 local ballots this month, these two hearings are the test of whether self-generated power changes the politics.
  • Finance: $74 billion is capex for a company that just told IPO investors AI revenue rose ninefold in Q3 while renting capacity to Google and Anthropic. Count it against the 15 GW Musk promised by end-2027.
  • Security: A 6 GW campus on a 250 MW rural cooperative with a 24 GWh battery is a grid-resilience story as much as a compute one. Watch who underwrites the upgrades.
  • Beginners: Elon Musk's SpaceX wants to spend $74 billion on two enormous AI computer sites that would make their own electricity; local residents in Arizona are pushing back.

Source: Reuters via The Star (Starbase) · Baxtel (Cochise County) · Reuters

A Microsoft 365 outage took Outlook, Teams calendars and Copilot down for most of Thursday, with Anthropic and OpenAI connectors failing alongside

Microsoft said a large number of servers became unexpectedly unavailable from around 5:15 a.m. AEDT on November 13, then that a core process handling secure connections was overwhelmed; it reverted a recent network configuration change and said there was no indication of malicious activity. Downdetector logged nearly 140,000 Outlook reports at the peak, seven in ten from the US. Microsoft 365 Copilot, Graph, Intune, Defender and Power BI were affected, Anthropic reported an upstream issue with its Microsoft 365 connector and OpenAI reported connector problems; recovery was still partial late in the day and a post-incident report is promised.

  • Executives: Every AI assistant wired to Microsoft 365 went down with it. If Copilot or a connector is in a workflow, the Microsoft dependency is the single point of failure, not the model.
  • Security: Defender, Intune and Purview were affected. Check your detection gaps for the window and treat the 48-hour email timeout as a delivery-integrity issue.
  • Developers: Graph was degraded for hours. Agents that call Graph need timeouts, retries with backoff and a degraded mode, not a crash.
  • Beginners: Microsoft's email, calendar and AI assistant stopped working for much of the world for most of a day because of a configuration change, not a hack.

Source: ABC News (Australia) live blog · BleepingComputer
